results.name: OverDrive Founder Steve Potash Steps Back; Marc DeBevoise Takes Over as CEO
results.content:
OverDrive founder Steve Potash (l) and newly appointed CEO Marc DeBevoise.
It's the end of an era at leading library vendor OverDrive. On June 23, the company announced that the company's founder and visionary Steve Potash has stepped back from his role as CEO, handing the reins to Marc DeBevoise, who joined the company roughly four months ago as President.
"OverDrive has extraordinary reach, incredible momentum, and an enduring mission—and I’m thrilled to lead this company forward," DeBevoise said. "I'm grateful to Steve for his continued partnership and to the Board for their confidence, and I look forward to working with our team and partners to build on everything this company stands for." The move comes just days ahead of the 2026 American Library Association Annual Conference, set to run from June 25-30 in Chicago, and as the library ebook market has entered a contentious new period, with several states and municipalities considering—and three so far passing—legislation designed to rein in what librarians say are unsustainable prices and license terms from the major publishers.
Among the headlines this week: the 2026 ALA Annual Conference kicks off next week; More response to the Authors Guild's take on digital library lending; a federal judge rebukes Trump's bid to censor signage at national parks; and Arkansans speak out against potential new library restrictions.
OverDrive founder Steve Potash (l) and newly appointed CEO Marc DeBevoise.

results.name: OverDrive enters next chapter with new CEO | Local News | clevelandjewishnews.com
results.content:
After serving as CEO of OverDrive for 40 years, Potash is transitioning to the role of board chairman and DeBevoise, a longtime senior executive in the streaming technology space, is taking over after spending the last three-plus months as the company’s first-ever president.
Jul 13, 2026 · Posted 4 hrs ago at 3: 00 PM · Facebook · Twitter · WhatsApp · SMS · Email · +1 · DeBevoise · +1 · Potash · Facebook · Twitter · WhatsApp · SMS · Email · Print · Copy article link · Save · OverDrive founder Steve Potash compared Marc DeBevoise, the company’s new CEO, to a certain space ranger currently on the big screen in theaters around the world.
After serving as CEO of OverDrive for 40 years, Potash is transitioning to the role of board chairman and DeBevoise, a longtime senior executive in the streaming technology space, is taking over after spending the last three-plus months as the company’s first-ever president.
OverDrive announced the transition in a news release June 23. “I’ve been in that combined industry of media and tech, and really my career for the past 25 years has been about evolving access to content,” DeBevoise, who previously held senior executive roles for CBS and ViacomCBS, which is now Paramount Global, and was the CEO of Brightcove Inc., a video hosting and streaming technology platform from March 2022 to February 2025, when it was acquired by Bending Spoons, an Italian technology company, told the CJN.
New York City-based private equity firm KKR & Co., purchased a controlling stake in OverDrive in June 2020 and Potash, 73, said in the last few years, conversations were had during board meetings with KKR in the last handful of years about a succession plan. “About two years ago, we started a national search for a CEO successor,” Potash said.

results.name: We do the hardest part of sales | OverDrive Group
results.content:
# We do the hardest part of sales  
Local media needs more local direct revenue than ever. But the old way of generating it doesn’t work like it used to.  
By Chris Overby, Founder & CEO, OverDrive Group · July 2026  
If you’ve been leading local media sales teams over the past few decades like I have, you’ve watched the job get harder.  
We need more local direct revenue than ever. National and regional dollars have shifted toward programmatic and digital platforms, and what’s left has to be built locally, one business at a time. At the same time, there are fewer people doing that work. More than half of broadcast sellers have left the industry over the last decade, and the sellers still here are carrying more accounts, more responsibility, and less time to go find new business.  
The old junior AE model doesn’t work like it used to either. Hiring young sellers to pound the phones, build a book, and earn their way up used to help fill the top of the funnel. But that job isn’t as attractive as it once was. The people who would’ve taken those roles ten years ago now have better options in digital and tech sales, and they’re taking them.  
So we’ve created a situation where the most important work in the building gets the least amount of time. And it also happens to be the hardest part of the job.
## Prospecting is a full-time job  
SaaS figured this out years ago. Software companies stopped pretending the same person should own every part of the sales process from cold prospecting to close. They broke the work apart. Prospecting became its own job. Closing became its own job. Customer growth became its own job.  
That doesn’t mean those jobs stopped working together. It means each part got the focus, tools, systems, and daily discipline it needed to work well. Local media has been slower to make that shift. We’ve kept asking account executives to prospect, pitch, close, service, renew, and grow accounts at the same time, and then we wonder why prospecting is the first thing to slip.  
But prospecting is a full-time job.
## That’s why I built OverDrive  
OverDrive Group brings the discipline of a real outbound team together with the fluency of people trained to talk about media the way media actually sells. We don’t sell lists. We land first meetings.  
We identify the right businesses, find the right decision-makers, call, email, follow up, track what’s happening, learn from what we’re hearing, and keep working until real meetings are on the calendar. And we do it under your brand.  
That last part matters. We’re not trying to replace your sellers. We’re building the front end of your pipeline so your sellers can spend more time doing what they’re best at: building relationships, proving value, closing business, and growing accounts.  
The old way depended on heroic effort. The new way depends on a system. That’s what we’ve built.  
> The bell still rings for the close. Our job is to make sure there’s a line of first meetings behind it.  
Chris Overby spent 25 years in local media before founding OverDrive Group in 2024. OverDrive Group books first meetings for radio, local TV, digital, out-of-home, publishing, and sports sellers, under their brand.

results.name: OverDrive Taps Digital Strategy Expert Marc DeBevoise
results.content:
Digital content provider OverDrive announced on March 3 that it has brought in Marc DeBevoise as its new president. DeBevoise, former CEO at the video platform Brightcove and a past leader at the online content network CBS Interactive, will help guide the company known for library reading app Libby, school “science of reading app” Sora, and video-streaming app Kanopy.  
OverDrive founder and CEO Steve Potash, who served as company president prior to DeBevoise’s appointment, [said in a statement](https://company.overdrive.com/2026/03/03/overdrive-names-marc-debevoise-president-expanding-support-for-libraries-and-schools/) that he expects DeBevoise to “make Libby, Sora, and Kanopy even more user friendly, more inclusive, and more joyful to use” and “help libraries and schools do what they do best, change lives through reading, viewing, and learning.” Potash and DeBevoise now will work together with the OverDrive leadership team.  
DeBevoise told *PW* that he’s excited to be at a mission-driven company, connecting “publishers and content studios and creators” with public institutions through digital media.  
“My career for the past 20-ish years has been about helping content find its audience, from the iPhone to the iPad to subscription streaming to free streaming,” he said. “OverDrive is a company that was on that same journey for a slightly different part of the media and content world.”
“My history has been in launching new things,” he added. “CBS All Access was the first network streaming service, and that became Paramount+. At Brightcove, we spent a lot of time revamping an AI suite to enable automated video publishing and metadata tagging and some of those key back-end features for a lot of our B2B companies, for our software customers.”  
Now, he said, he looks forward to “continuing the evolution of our products”—Libby, Sora, and Kanopy—with OverDrive’s tech team. A top priority will be “broadening the content and the way we think about the content that we serve” to libraries, K–12 schools, and universities, he said, although he has only begun to strategize with product developers.  
[Overdrive](https://company.overdrive.com/company-profile/who-we-are/), a Cleveland-based certified B Corp founded in 1986, serves more than 80,000 libraries and schools in 115 countries. Another goal for the months ahead, DeBevoise said, would be “overall global expansion. In the U.S., we are absolutely the number one provider in this space,” yet there appears to be room for growth worldwide. “We’re typically a non-exclusive partner to an international library system, and there are other competitors in there, so I think there’s a lot of opportunity.”  
*This article has been updated.*
